answers.answer: A fresh id per call is the single shot pattern: each run is independent and joins no accumulated state. Reusing the same id is the conversational memory pattern: state such as chat history accumulates across invocations because every run joins the same thread. With no thread id there is no primary key for storing and retrieving checkpoints, so the checkpointer cannot save state, cannot resume after an interrupt, and cannot support time travel debugging.
accept: a unique id per run keeps executions independent (single shot)
reusing one id accumulates state across invocations, which is how conversational memory works
thread_id is the primary key for storing and retrieving checkpoints
without it the checkpointer cannot save state or resume after an interrupt

answers.answer: The next field holds the node names to execute next, and an empty tuple means the graph is complete. The config field addresses an individual checkpoint: it contains thread_id, checkpoint_ns, and checkpoint_id, so the thread id alone names the thread while the checkpoint id names one point inside it. Credit also for noting that values holds the state channel values and metadata holds source, writes, and the step counter.
accept: next holds the node names to execute next
an empty tuple in next means the graph is complete
config addresses a checkpoint and contains thread_id, checkpoint_ns and checkpoint_id
the checkpoint_id is what distinguishes one checkpoint from the thread as a whole

answers.answer: Exactly four. An empty checkpoint with START as the next node, one holding the user input with node_a next, one holding node_a's outputs with node_b next, and one holding node_b's outputs with no next nodes. The count is four rather than two because a checkpoint is written at each super-step boundary, a super-step is one tick in which all nodes scheduled for that step run, and the input is its own super-step alongside node_a and node_b.
accept: exactly four checkpoints
one per super-step: the input, node_a, and node_b, plus the initial empty one with START next
a checkpoint is written at each super-step boundary
a super-step is one tick in which all nodes scheduled for that step execute, potentially in parallel

answers.answer: Nodes before that checkpoint are skipped because their results are already saved. Nodes after it re-execute, and that re-execution includes LLM calls, API requests, and interrupts, which are always re-triggered during replay. So resuming costs full price for everything on the far side of the boundary: the same tokens, the same outbound requests. Credit for adding that within a single super-step, successful node writes are persisted as tasks and are not recomputed when a sibling node fails.
accept: nodes before the checkpoint are skipped because their results are saved
nodes after the checkpoint re-execute
the re-execution includes LLM calls, API requests and interrupts
resuming is not free: the cost falls on everything after the checkpoint

answers.answer: With a checkpointer attached, a resumed run re-executes every node after the checkpoint, so the insert runs a second time and the row is duplicated. Re-execution is ordinary operation rather than an error path. Node logic has to be written so that running it twice does not corrupt state: a node that inserts a row should not create duplicate rows unless that is intended, which in practice means an idempotency key, an upsert, or a check before the write.
accept: replay re-executes nodes after the checkpoint, so the node runs twice
running it twice duplicates the row
node logic must be designed so re-execution does not corrupt state
the fix is idempotency: a derived key, an upsert, or a conditional write

answers.answer: Execution resumes from the start of the node and re-executes all of its logic, not from the line after the interrupt call. The expensive summary is therefore computed a second time. Mechanically, the first interrupt invocation in the node raises GraphInterrupt, halting execution and sending the provided value to the client, and the client resumes by supplying a value through the Command primitive. A checkpointer must be enabled, because the feature relies on persisting the graph state.
accept: the graph resumes from the start of the node and re-executes all its logic
the summary is recomputed, so work before the interrupt call is repeated
the first interrupt call raises GraphInterrupt and surfaces the value to the client
resuming uses the Command primitive to supply a value
a checkpointer must be enabled because the feature relies on persisted state

answers.answer: sync persists changes synchronously before the next step starts. async persists them asynchronously while the next step executes. exit persists only when the graph exits. Under exit, a run killed partway through has not written its intermediate steps. That bears on replay, which resumes from a prior checkpoint, and on interrupt, which relies on the graph state having been persisted.
accept: sync persists before the next step starts
async persists while the next step executes
exit persists only when the graph exits
under exit an interrupted run has no intermediate checkpoints written
replay needs a prior checkpoint and interrupt relies on persisted state
